The app is plain HTML, CSS and ES modules, with no build step. Browsers do not load modules

```
index.html              markup only
css/                    one file per area, linked in cascade order (responsive.css last)
js/
  main.js               entry point (and the Claude artifact hot-reload hook)
  app.js                App: composition root and mediator between model, services and views
  core/                 util (random, clamp…), Emitter (observer), storage
  data/                 tables: SuperCollider scales, tunings, Coypu world rhythms
  theory/               pure music theory: consonance, spelling, scale context, chords
  sequencer/            pure pattern logic: timeline, rhythm, roles, melody
                        + Session, the model all edits go through
  export/coypu.js       the session as a Coypu script
  persistence/          snapshot / restore (memento, v1 and v2)
  audio/                AudioEngine (Web Audio facade), voices (one strategy per lane),

```

- **`js/`** has 31 modules in layers. Each layer only uses the ones below it:

| Layer | Contents |
|---|---|
| `core/`, `data/` | helpers, an event emitter, localStorage; the scale, tuning and rhythm tables (copied unchanged) |
| `theory/` | consonance, note spelling, scale context, chords. No state and no page code. |
| `sequencer/` | timeline, rhythm, roles, melody generation, and **`Session`**, the one object that holds the pattern and all edits |
| `export/`, `persistence/` | Coypu script export; save and restore of the session |
| `audio/` | `AudioEngine`, `voices`, the worker clock, `Transport` (scheduler) |
| `midi/` | `MidiOutput`: notes, pitch bend, clock, port choice |
| `ui/` | one view per part of the page, plus `LaneInput` (taps, drags, Shift+arrows), keyboard shortcuts, toast, code dialog |
| `app.js`, `main.js` | `App` connects everything; `main.js` starts it and keeps the Claude hot-reload hook |

## Design patterns used
- **Mediator:** `App` is the only module that connects the others. Before, audio, MIDI and the page all called each other through shared globals (`state`, `AC`, `midi`, `playing`, `toast`). Those globals are gone.
- **Observer:** `Transport` and `MidiOutput` send events (play state, playhead position, port changes, messages). The views listen for them, so the audio and MIDI code never touch the page.
- **Facade:** `AudioEngine` hides the Web Audio setup. Callers just ask to play a voice, mute a lane or set the delay.
- **Strategy:** each lane's synth (saw, square, triangle) is a separate function behind the same interface.
- **Memento:** saving and restoring a session lives in `persistence/snapshot.js`, including loading old v1 saves.
- **Model:** `Session` holds all the edit logic and has no page or audio code.

I kept the music logic (theory, rhythm, melody) as plain functions rather than wrapping it in classes. It doesn't need any state, and that makes it easy to test.

- **Same output:** I ran the original inline code and the new modules side by side with the same seeded random numbers, over 400 seeds. Each run went through roll → pattern length → lane length → step and duration edits → reroll → regenerate. The Coypu exports and saved state were identical every time, as was the order of the random draws. Saving and reloading reproduced the same export every time.
- **Browser test:** in headless Chrome, both versions loaded the page and behaved identically through roll, pattern length, step toggle, lane length, mute, play (playhead moving), Space to stop, and copy. Both logged only one harmless warning: Chrome blocks phone vibration on simulated clicks.

I removed the `@logic-start`/`@logic-end` markers from the old file, since the logic now lives in its own modules and can be imported directly. Physical MIDI devices weren't available to test; that code was moved without changing its logic. # About Juggler

This is Juggler's own reference manual — factual information about the Juggler
application itself. Use it to answer questions about what Juggler is, how it
works, and how to drive it. It does not describe the user's own code or project.

## What Juggler is

Juggler is a visual workbench for AI coding agents: see and control your coding
agent, locally or remotely. Work in the desktop app, or run the juggler server
on a dev box and open the same live session from the app or a browser; several
clients can attach at once.

- **A real desktop GUI.** Finder-style Miller columns; tool calls, context and
  properties open into their own views.
- **The session is a tree, not a doom-scroll.** A conversation is a persistent
  Yjs document: branch nested threads, move or copy items between branches, and
  undo structural changes. It survives a quit, approvals waiting included.
- **You see what the model saw.** Any recorded LLM transaction opens to show its
  system prompt, messages, tool definitions, output, token and cache use.
- **Plugins all the way down.** Tools, commands, strategies, pins, workspaces
  and hooks are JavaScript extensions you can inspect, fork or replace.
- **Vendor-neutral.** Hosted APIs, agent CLIs you already have, or local models,
  switchable mid-conversation. No house model, no resold tokens, no account.

## Core concepts

- **Conversation** — a Yjs document holding the tree of messages, threads and
  context items; attached clients stay in sync.
- **Threads** — sub-conversations branched off a point in the tree, for a
  tangent, a delegated sub-task or a competing approach; a child works in
  isolation and returns its result to the parent. Each opens as its own column,
  where you can message it, approve its plan or tool calls, answer its
  questions and carry it on after it finishes; what it does later reaches the
  parent too.
- **Context items** — the typed units of context (files, tool calls, memory, the
  system prompt, dropped files). Each is a plugin with its own UI, and every
  tool the model can call is backed by one.
- **Strategies** — pluggable loop policies that gate which tools are offered and
  how calls are approved, without changing the cached system prompt.

## Pinboard

A tabbed panel behind the right edge of the window. Each tab is a "pin" supplied
by an extension; pins belong to the project session, so every viewer sees the
same board. A pin is only a view: pinning a file shows it to you, not to the
model, and the agent can request a pin but cannot list or read the board.
Built-in pins:

- **Plan** and **Todos** — the plan or checklist of the thread you are reading,
  else of the nearest parent with one. Read-only; they change through their tools.
- **Git** — review changes: each repository's branch and drift from upstream,
  and every changed file's diff, for the project or the visible conversation's
  workspace. Working tree against HEAD by default, or staged, a branch, the last
  commit or any git diff range. Line comments go to the conversation as one
  message. It reads git, so edits made by hand show too.
- **Memory** — the project facts the assistant keeps.
- **Running tasks** — every command the project's conversations are running now,
  background or foreground, grouped by conversation, each with a Stop and a link
  to the action that started it.
- **File** — a live file or directory (an agent-made pin is held to the project).
- **Project files** — the project's files as a tree, everything on disk.
- **Environment** — the variables commands run with in this project, and the
  approval for the project's committed env file (see "Environment variables").

An HTML file is shown as its rendered page wherever a file is displayed (a pin, a
read or write result, a dropped file), in a sandboxed frame that cannot reach
Juggler, with a Source button. So the agent can show you a report or mock-up by
writing an HTML file in the project and pinning it.

## Tools the agent can use

Availability depends on enabled extensions and capabilities, and the strategy
may withhold some. Juggler Core provides:

- **read**, **write**, **edit** (exact-string replacement), **glob** (files by
  name), **grep** (ripgrep content search), **batch_read / batch_grep**.
- **bash** — a command in a fresh shell rooted at the project; nothing persists
  between calls (standing variables go in the env files). Can run in background.
- **Monitor** — a background command whose output lines stream in as events.
- **TaskOutput / TaskStop** (alias KillShell) — read or stop a background task.
- **query_code** — JavaScript over a read-only view of the codebase; only the
  returned value and console.log output enter context; image(path) attaches one.
- **run_code** — a JavaScript program that also calls the conversation's tools.
  Only its return value and a list of its changes enter context. Each call is
  approved as if made directly; one awaiting approval pauses the program and a
  denial ends it. Its description names the tools a program cannot call.
- **WebFetch** — a URL as markdown (15-minute cache), or an image as an image;
  given a prompt, a sub-agent reads the page and returns only the answer.
- **WebSearch** — web search returning titles, URLs and descriptions.
- **Explore** / **Research** — sub-agents that investigate the codebase
  (read-only) or the web and return only their findings.
- **create_thread** — a self-contained sub-task in an isolated thread, which
  the user can open and steer.
- **new_conversation** — an independent peer conversation in its own tab.
- **todo** — a lightweight checklist; **plan** — an approval-gated plan whose
  steps are then tracked.
- **memory** — remember or forget durable project facts.
- **skill** — load an Agent Skill on demand.
- **pin_to_pinboard** — show something on the Pinboard.
- **AskUserQuestion** — structured multiple-choice questions for the user.
- **define_command** — save a prompt as a custom /name command (user-approved).

Other built-in extensions add **AboutJuggler** (this manual),
**ReadJugglerSource** (the app's SDK and example-extension source), MCP server
tools plus **McpRestartServer** (restart one MCP server, offered once a server is
configured), and **exa_search** (Exa web search; needs an Exa API key in its
settings).

## Strategies

- **Default** — standard general-purpose coding-assistant behaviour.
- **Auto-approve** — like Default, but a cheap model auto-approves routine
  prompts it is sure are safe, so you are asked only about risky ones (review
  level balanced, relaxed or custom, in Juggler Core's settings).
- **Read-only** — any action that may change files is automatically refused.
- **YOLO** — auto-approves every tool use. Use at your own risk.

Switch with the strategy switcher (default Shift+Tab; hold for a menu).

## Approvals

A tool call that needs permission shows a card with these buttons:

- **Yes** approves just this call.
- **Yes + Don't Ask Again for <pattern>** also saves that pattern, for example
  "make *", for this conversation. Click the pencil on the button to edit the
  pattern. The permissions button ("Edits on" / "Edits off", in the line of
  settings under the message box with the strategy and model; above the text
  on a touch screen) lists saved patterns and allowed folders. There you can
  edit them, add patterns for all conversations, and turn file edits on or off
  (⌘E on macOS).
- **No** refuses this call. It also refuses every other call waiting with it and
  stops the turn.

To stop being asked, switch strategy: **Auto-approve** has a cheap model approve
routine calls, and **YOLO** approves everything. This is the quickest way to let
a multi-step job such as a rebuild run. If you keep approving within one turn,
the card offers both. Switching there, or with Shift+Tab, also decides the calls
already waiting.

## Slash commands

Type "/" in the composer. Built in: **/new** (new empty conversation),
**/duplicate** (clone this one), **/clear** (clear messages), **/compact**
(fold older turns into a summary thread, keeping recent ones as Settings →
Defaults → Keep recent conversation says; **/compact all** folds everything),
**/handoff** (summarise into a new
conversation to continue), **/thread** (new sub-conversation thread),
**/export** (save as an HTML page to share), **/commands** (manage custom
commands), **/init** (have the agent survey the project and draft an
AGENTS.md), **/shell** (run a shell command yourself). Juggler MCP adds **/mcp**
(list servers; /mcp restart <name> restarts one).

**Running a command yourself**: start a message with "!" ("! npm run lint" is
the same as "/shell npm run lint"). The command is posted to the conversation
as an ordinary bash tool call, with no approval card and no model call: select
it to watch its output, and stop it with Stop command in its properties panel
(the same button stops any running bash call). The model sees the call and its
result with your next message. If a turn is running, the command waits for the
turn's next boundary. A "!" on its own is an ordinary message.

**Custom commands** need no code: a markdown file of YAML frontmatter over a
prompt template, hot-reloaded on save. "$1".."$9" are positional arguments,
"$ARGUMENTS" everything after the name as typed, "$$" a literal dollar. Run
modes: send, insert as an editable draft, or run in a sub-thread (with its own
strategy or model if set). Create one by typing an unknown name (the menu offers
"New command…"), with /commands, or by asking the assistant. Files live in
~/.juggler/commands/ or <project>/.juggler/commands/ (shared through git); a
project command shadows a user one, and neither overrides a built-in.

## Agent Skills

A skill follows the open Agent Skills standard (agentskills.io): a folder with a
SKILL.md (YAML frontmatter plus markdown), optionally scripts/, references/ and
assets/. Only names and descriptions are listed; the skill tool loads a body
when a task matches. Discovered at:

- <project>/.juggler/skills/<name>/SKILL.md and <project>/.agents/skills/...
- <config>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md (~/.juggler/skills/) and ~/.agents/skills/...

The .agents paths are cross-agent aliases. Files in a skill are read through the
ordinary read and bash tools under normal approval — no new access path.

## Tool hooks

A hook applies around every tool call whatever the strategy: beforeTool (deny
the call, make it ask you, or add a note) or afterTool (add a note to the
result). Hook files are no-code markdown in ~/.juggler/hooks/ — user scope only,
never from a project — with frontmatter for description, event, and optional
tool, input/result patterns, isError, verdict (deny or ask) and repeat. A hook
file can never allow a call. Extensions can provide code hooks. Deny beats ask
beats allow, and a hook's ask overrides even YOLO. A call's properties show the
hooks that acted on it.

## Workspaces

A workspace is where a conversation's tools run — where bash executes and what
file tools are relative to. Every project is one already. Built-in providers:

- **Group** — only organises conversations; they work in the project, nothing is
  created on disk. Ungrouping returns them; deleting it bins them.
- **Git Worktree** — another branch in a tree of its own. Files are separate;
  ports, databases and the machine are not, and the first build is a full one.
- **Scratch Copy** — a throwaway copy of the tree, git or not, minus what
  .gitignore excludes. Applying back copies whole files and refuses any the
  project has changed since.
- **Subfolder** — work in one folder of a monorepo; the rest stays readable.
  Nothing is created or removed. Closing it returns or bins its conversations.

Create one with "New workspace or group". Several conversations can share one,
and it can outlive them. Its conversations sit in a box in the tab strip, with a
dot for uncommitted work and a "+" for a new conversation there. Selecting the
box opens a panel: the place, its path, its state, and the provider's ways of
finishing (a worktree offers commit or discard; discard deletes tree and
branch). Closing a workspace bins its conversations; the Bin restores them. To
move a conversation, drag its tab to another box or the flat strip (the project
folder) and confirm; a move within the same tree, such as into a group, needs no
confirmation. Providers are extension-declared files
(workspaces/*-workspace-provider.js), so adding one needs no rebuild; every
workspace is a tree on the machine the server runs on.

## Keyboard shortcuts

Shortcuts are customisable. The current bindings for this platform:

**Conversations**

- ⌘J — Jump to conversation needing attention: Switch to the next conversation waiting on you; select its first pending approval, or scroll to the end if it just needs a look.
- ⌘N or ⌥N — New conversation: Create a new conversation and switch to it.
- ⇧⌘N — New window: Open a new app window. Desktop app only — in a plain browser tab the key is left to the browser.
- ⌥⌘↑ or ⇞ — Previous conversation: Switch to the conversation above in the tab list (wraps around).
- ⌥⌘↓ or ⇟ — Next conversation: Switch to the conversation below in the tab list (wraps around).
- ⇧⇞ — Move conversation up: Move the current conversation one place up the tab list, within its own workspace box.
- ⇧⇟ — Move conversation down: Move the current conversation one place down the tab list, within its own workspace box.
- ⌥↑ — Select previous item: Move the selection to the item above in the conversation, without leaving the message box.
- ⌥↓ — Select next item: Move the selection to the item below in the conversation, without leaving the message box.
- ⌘⌫ — Move conversation to bin: Move the current conversation to the bin.
- ⌘E — Toggle file edit permission: Allow or ask-before file edits for the current conversation.
- F2 — Rename conversation: Rename the current conversation (opens the tab’s inline name editor). Also on Return when the tab bar itself is focused.
- ⇧⎋ — Pause conversation: Stops as soon as possible without interrupting any tool uses or in-flight LLM responses. Trades places with plain Escape under some Escape-key behaviours (see below).
- ⇧⇥ — Switch strategy: Cycle the active strategy; hold to open the strategy menu.
- ⌥⌘M — Switch model: Cycle through recently-used models; hold to open the model menu.
- ⌥⌘T — Switch thinking level: Cycle the current model’s thinking level; hold to open the level popover.
- ⌥⇧⌘M — Open model picker: Open the model picker and leave it open, so the list can be read rather than cycled. Type to filter, arrows to move, Enter to pick, Escape to close.

**Projects**

- ⇧⌘J — Jump to conversation needing attention, any project: Go to the next conversation waiting on you in any project on this computer, opening its project if it is not this one.
- ⌘K — Switch session: Open the list of sessions at this one, to pick with the arrow keys and Return. Keep the modifier held and press K again to walk on through the open sessions, then the recent projects; let go to switch, or press Escape to stay.

**Search**

- ⌘F — Find: Open the find bar to search for text in the panel you are in.

**Editing**

- ⌘Z — Undo: Undo the last change in the current conversation.
- ⇧⌘Z — Redo: Redo the last undone change in the current conversation.

**View**

- ⌘+ — Zoom in: Increase the interface zoom level.
- ⌘− — Zoom out: Decrease the interface zoom level.
- ⌥⌘G — Group consecutive tool uses: Collapse runs of adjacent tool uses into a single group item, or show them individually again.
- ⌥⌘P — Toggle Pinboard: Open or close the pinboard — the tabbed panel of pinned items behind the right edge of the window.
- ⌥⌘← or ⌘⇞ — Previous pin: Show the pinboard tab to the left. Plain ← does the same when the board has focus and nothing inside the pin wants the key; this chord works wherever focus is.
- ⌥⌘→ or ⌘⇟ — Next pin: Show the pinboard tab to the right. Plain → does the same when the board has focus and nothing inside the pin wants the key; this chord works wherever focus is.
- ⌘/ — Show keyboard shortcuts: Open Settings to this Keyboard shortcuts tab.

## Model providers

- **Anthropic (API)**, **Anthropic (Claude Code CLI)**
- **OpenAI ChatGPT**, **OpenAI Codex (ChatGPT plan)**
- **Google Gemini**, **GitHub Copilot**, **Mistral AI**, **Moonshot Kimi**,
  **DeepSeek**, **Z.AI GLM**, **OpenRouter**, **OpenCode Zen**
- **ACP Agents** (external agents speaking the Agent Client Protocol)
- **Ollama (local)**, **LM Studio (local)**, **llama.cpp (local)**,
  **LocalAI (local)**
- **Jev (TypeSafe)** — a decision model answering yes/no, choice and score
  questions (e.g. judging tool approvals); not usable for chat.

Plus any number of **custom endpoints** (gateways, tenants, regions, local
servers), each with its own base URL, credentials, headers and models, and each
its own provider in the picker. Keys are stored locally.

## Configuration and data locations

Per-user state lives in ~/.juggler:

- **credentials.json** — API keys, owner-only. **default-model.json** — your
  default model. **custom-providers.json** — your custom endpoints.
- **env.json** — variables for every command, in every project.
- **env-approvals.json** — the project env.json contents you approved.
- **workspace.json** — the desktop app's open windows and theme.
- **extensions/**, **commands/**, **hooks/**, **skills/** — your extensions,
  custom commands, hook files and Agent Skills.
- **cache/** — regenerable (recent projects, learned context sizes); safe to
  delete.

Everything directly under ~/.juggler is durable and worth copying to a new
machine; cache/ is not. Logs are elsewhere (see Troubleshooting).
JUGGLER_CONFIG_DIR moves ~/.juggler and JUGGLER_LOG_DIR the logs.

Per-project state lives in <project>/.juggler: MEMORY.md (the memory tool's
project facts, private to your checkout), commands/, skills/, env.json and
env.local.json, plus config, session, conversation folders, MCP config and bash
output. That location is fixed; a checkout that must not be written to has to
exclude the folder.

### Environment variables

Every command (foreground, background, Monitor, Python) gets variables from
three JSON files of names to values, merged in this order, later winning:

- ~/.juggler/env.json — yours, in every project.
- <project>/.juggler/env.json — the project's, meant to be committed. Applies
  only once you approve its exact contents in the Environment pin, and asks
  again after any change. Your own two files are never gated.
- <project>/.juggler/env.local.json — yours, in this project; the place for

## Extensions

Built in: Juggler Core (@juggler/core — tools, strategies, commands, pins,
viewers, workspace providers), Juggler MCP (@juggler/mcp), Exa Search
(@juggler/exa) and About Juggler (@juggler/about — this manual; turning it off
removes this tool). User extensions go in ~/.juggler/extensions/. The Extensions
view toggles each extension and capability and edits their settings.

### Writing an extension

No source checkout is needed; the binary has an "ext" subcommand:

- "juggler ext init <name>" — scaffold an extension (manifest, sample tool,
  strategy and command, README) that loads unedited.
- "juggler ext validate <path>" — the app's admission check (required fields,
  engineApi compatibility) plus that every "provides" glob matches files.
- "juggler ext link <path>" — symlink into ~/.juggler/extensions/; saves then
  hot-reload it in connected viewers.
- "juggler ext add github.com/owner/repo" — git-clone a published extension.

An extension is a folder with a juggler.extension.json manifest and capability
files named with a type suffix, which the manifest's globs match:

- context-items/*-context-item.js — tools ("juggler/context-item")
- strategies/*-strategy-type.js — loop policies ("juggler/strategy-type")
- commands/*-command-type.js — slash commands ("juggler/command-type")
- cards/*-card.js — sidebar info tiles ("juggler/info-card-type")
- pins/*-pin.js — Pinboard tabs ("juggler/pinboard-item-type"); an optional
  pins/*-pin.meta.js descriptor lets the agent pin one
- viewers/*-file-viewer.js — how a file type is shown ("juggler/file-viewer")
- workspaces/*-workspace-provider.js — places to work
  ("juggler/workspace-provider")
- hooks/*-hook.js — tool hooks ("juggler/hook-type")

Each capability is a default-exported class extending its SDK base class, with a
static MANIFEST. An extension may also contribute one system-prompt module and
declare "settings" (typed values including secrets, read at runtime with
extensionConfigResolve from "juggler/ops").

Minimal manifest. Required: id, name, version, provides; engineApi is
recommended (checked against web/sdk/version.js); unknown keys are an error:

    {
      "id": "@you/word-count",
      "name": "Word Count",
      "version": "1.0.0",
      "engineApi": "^1.0.0",
      "provides": { "contextItems": ["context-items/*-context-item.js"] }
    }

Minimal tool: getToolDefinitions() (the schema), execute() (return RAW data)
and getSummary(). The most common mistake is reading outcome.foo instead of
outcome.result.foo — execute()'s return value is outcome.result:

    import ContextItem from '/worker-module?url=%2Fsdk%2Fcontext-item.js';

    class WordCountContextItem extends ContextItem {
      static MANIFEST = { id: 'word-count', name: 'Word Count', version: '1.0.0',
        description: 'Count words in a text string' };

      static getToolDefinitions() {
        return [{
          name: 'word_count',
          category: 'read',
          description: 'Count words in a text string',
          input_schema: { type: 'object',
            properties: { text: { type: 'string', description: 'Text to count' } },
            required: ['text'] }
        }];
      }

      async execute(params) {
        return { count: params.text.split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean).length };
      }

      getSummary(outcome) {
        if (!outcome.success) return { summary: outcome.error, success: false };

## Updates and connectivity

Juggler contacts the network when it needs to: LLM requests go to the provider
you configured, WebFetch/WebSearch reach the sites you ask for, enabled
extensions may reach the hosts they declare, and Juggler checks for new
versions. Model traffic goes straight from the machine Juggler's server runs on
to the provider you chose; Juggler does not proxy it.

All of these connections follow one proxy setting, in Settings → Connectivity →
Outbound proxy: System (the default; honours HTTPS_PROXY, HTTP_PROXY and
NO_PROXY, then the OS proxy), Direct, or Manual (a URL you enter). Loopback
addresses always go direct. Three variables are read from Juggler's own
environment when its server starts, not from the env.json files (those reach
commands only). On macOS an app opened from the Dock does not read the shell
profile, so set them with launchctl setenv or start Juggler from a terminal:

- **SSL_CERT_FILE** / **SSL_CERT_DIR** — trust a proxy's certificate authority.
  On macOS and Windows setting either one REPLACES the system certificate store
  (CAs only in the Keychain or Windows store, such as a company's, stop
  counting), so the file must also hold the public roots for any connection
  that bypasses the proxy; GODEBUG=x509sslcertoverrideplatform=0 makes those
  platforms ignore both. On Linux they replace the default bundle file and the
  default directories respectively.
- **JUGGLER_CODEX_BASE_URL** — replaces https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex
  for every Codex request (turns, model list, usage). $NAME in it is expanded.
  It must be https, or http to a loopback host, with no user name, password,
  query or fragment. An unusable value stops Codex with an error naming the
  variable; it never falls back to chatgpt.com.

A Codex access token that is not a JWT (such as a credential proxy's
placeholder) is sent as it is, and the backend decides. docs/network.md covers
running behind a TLS-intercepting or credential-injecting proxy.

how are melodies from scales generated ? just randomly? or something more special

Not just random. It's **weighted random**: for every note, each possible pitch gets a score from music rules, and then one is drawn by chance, with higher-scored pitches more likely. Good notes are likely and bad ones rare, but nothing is fixed, so each roll sounds different but still musical.

It runs in this order:

### 1. Scale and root
A random scale (from SuperCollider's 108) is put on a random root. `theory/scale-context.js` works out the note names. For Partch just-intonation scales, the root note isn't always the strongest note, so it picks as tonic the note most consonant with the rest.

### 2. Harmony (one chord per bar)
`theory/chords.js`
- **Chord on each scale note:** in 7-note scales, the usual stacked thirds. In other scales, it picks whichever notes sound most like a third and a fifth.
- **Progression:** it starts on the tonic. The next chords are weighted by how far their root moves: up a 4th or 5th is most likely, then ♭VII, ♭VI, vi, ♭III, and so on. Chords with a weak fifth or third are less likely.
- **Repeats:** a 4-bar phrase repeats for longer patterns. Half the time the last bar changes, like a turnaround.

### 3. Rhythm comes before pitch
`sequencer/rhythm.js`
Each lane gets either a world rhythm from Coypu (clave, tresillo, bembé…) or a random one where each step fires with one set probability. The Rhythm source slider decides which is more likely.

### 4. Pitch: the actual "melody brain"
`sequencer/melody.js` → `noteWeights`
For each note, every scale pitch in the lane's range is scored by multiplying these factors:

| Factor | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Consonance with the chord** | A curve with peaks at pure intervals (fifth, thirds, fourth…), so it also works for quarter tones and just intonation. Chord tones get a bonus. |
| **Beat strength** | On strong beats consonance counts more. Off-beats allow passing notes. |
| **Against the other lanes** | Bass is generated first. The mid lane is scored against the bass, the lead against both, and the lead avoids doubling the mid. |
| **Melodic motion** | Steps are preferred and big leaps fade out. After a leap it prefers stepping back the other way (classic leap recovery). Repeated notes are penalised. |
| **Bass rules** | The bass likes repeats, octaves, 4ths and 5ths, and lands on the chord root at the start of each bar 85% of the time. |
| **Up/down forms** | Scales with a different descending form (like melodic minor) only use the right notes in each direction. |
| **Register** | A bell curve keeps each voice near its centre: bass low, mid around B3, lead around C♯5. |
| **Loop closure** | The last note is chosen to lead smoothly back to the first. |
| **Lanes of different lengths** | If a 13-step lane hears the same step over several chords, the note has to fit all of them. One bad clash pulls its score down. |

The scores are then sharpened (raised to a power, so strong candidates win more often), and one pitch is drawn.

### 5. Durations
A note is usually held until the next one, up to a limit per voice. Occasionally it gets a long note, more likely on strong beats. The gate decides how much of each length actually sounds.

In short, it's close to a light version of rule-based counterpoint (species counterpoint, done with probabilities): harmony first, then rhythm, then the bass, then the voices above it, each scored by consonance, voice leading and register before a random pick.

The **−/+ buttons now shift the lane's pattern one step left or right**, and the length stays on the dropdown.

Each lane's controls now read **Steps [16] · Shift − + · Gate [50%]**. In the browser, the Square lane `C♯4 . C♯4 . … G♯3 . E4` became `E4 C♯4 . C♯4 . … G♯3 .` after `+`. The last note wrapped around to step 1, and the length stayed at 16.

**How it works**
- **Within its own loop:** the shift wraps around the lane's own length, not the pattern's. So a 13-step lane rotates within 13 steps, matching how the lanes cycle against each other.
- **Notes move whole:** each note keeps its pitch, velocity and held length.
- **Hidden steps stay put:** steps beyond the lane's current length don't move, so making the lane longer again still brings back the same steps.
- **Marked as edited:** the lane gets the "edited" tag. The Coypu export then writes out the exact gates (`#(…) asSeq`) instead of the world rhythm's name, because the name would no longer match.
- **Pitches aren't re-picked:** the notes keep their pitches when they move. That's what an offset normally means, but a note can end up against a different chord. Reroll the lane if a shift sounds off.

tools.description:
Attach something to the user’s Pinboard and bring it into view. This is a one-way display action: you cannot list or read the user’s existing pins, and repeating a request reveals the existing pin instead of adding another.

Choose the type that is *for* the thing you are showing, not the one that will accept it — several types accept a path, and the specific one knows how to run, render or summarize what is at the end of it.

It is also how to show the user something you have made rather than describe it: write it to a file in the project and pin that file. An HTML file is shown as the rendered page, scripts running, with its source a click away — so a report, chart or mock-up can be looked at, not just read.

Installed types:
- `env` — The environment variables every shell command gets in this project (from ~/.juggler/env.json, .juggler/env.json once approved, and .juggler/env.local.json), with the approval for the committed file. Show it when the user wants to set, check or approve one. No parameters.
- `git` — The git working tree — branch, status, changed files — of the project, or of the workspace the visible conversation works in, for review. Optionally scoped to another comparison: staged changes, a branch, a commit range. Parameters: `scope` (string) — What to compare. A preset — @uncommitted (default: working tree against HEAD), @staged, @unstaged, @branch (working tree against where the branch left main/master), @last (the last commit) — or a git diff expression: main...HEAD, main..feature, HEAD~3, --merge-base main, --cached [rev], --worktree.
- `memory` — The durable project facts kept in memory. No parameters.
- `plan` — The current plan and how far through it the conversation has got. No parameters.
- `tasks` — Every command this project's conversations are running, background or foreground, grouped by conversation. No parameters.
- `todo` — The current todo checklist. No parameters.
- `file` — Any file or directory, shown as its contents. The general case: reach for it when nothing above describes what the path actually holds. Parameters: `path` (string, required) — File or directory path, absolute or relative to the project. `isDirectory` (boolean) — Whether the path names a directory. A trailing slash also implies this.

A type installed after this list was built is accepted too: use its id and give it whatever parameters it expects, and it will validate its own config.

parameters.description: Parameters for the requested type, as listed above. Pass an empty object for a type that takes none.

type.description: Which kind of Pinboard item to add — the id of one of the installed types listed above.

tools.description: Run JavaScript against a read-only view of the codebase. Collapses many reads, greps and globs into one call — only the value you return, plus anything you print with `console.log`, enters context.

code.description:
JavaScript to execute (async/await OK; must return a value). Browser realm, NOT Node: no `process`/`require`/`Buffer`. In-scope bindings:
- `fs` — read-only fs.promises subset
- `path` — POSIX path (forward-slash, even on Windows)
- `grep(pattern, {cwd?, glob?, maxResults?, ignoreCase?})` → [{file, line, content}]
- `glob(pattern, {cwd?})` → string[]
- `projectRoot` — absolute root of the tree you are working in (forward-slashed). `import()` any JavaScript/JSON module under it by absolute path (e.g. `${projectRoot}/src/foo.js`) to call its real exports.
- `await image(path)` — attach a PNG/JPEG/GIF/WebP file to your result, so you see it

tools.description:
Answer a question from the web with a sub-agent and get back only the answer. It searches, reads as many pages as it needs, and checks them against the version actually installed in this project; none of those pages enter this conversation.
Use it when the answer takes several sources — API behaviour, what changed between versions, how a library is meant to be used. For one page whose URL you know, `WebFetch` with a `prompt` is cheaper; for questions about this codebase, use `Explore`.
The task must be self-contained: the sub-agent sees nothing of this conversation.

goal.description: Very short, single-line, user-facing label (for example, "Check React 20 changes"). Not the task or the return requirements.

session.description: Optional Research session name from an earlier call — continues that same research; omit it to start fresh.

task.description: What to find out, stated in full — including the library, version, or platform it concerns.

thoroughness.description: How much effort to spend before answering: "quick" for a first solid answer, "medium" (default) to corroborate it, "thorough" to be exhaustive.

tools.name: Research

tools.description:
Run a JavaScript program that calls tools; only what it returns enters the conversation, plus a list of what it changed. Use it for work that loops, branches or aggregates over many tool calls. Each call is approved as if you made it directly, and a denial ends the program. One that waits for the user's approval pauses the program until they answer.

`await tools.<name>({...})` calls any tool in your tool list by its name, with the same arguments, and resolves to its result text or throws its error, which the program may catch. Not callable from a program: Explore, plan, query_code, Research, create_thread, todo, WebFetch, drop_context_items. `await describeTool(name)` gives a tool's description and arguments; `describeTool()` lists them all.

code.description: JavaScript (async/await OK; return a value). Browser realm, not Node. In scope: `fs` (read-only fs.promises subset), `path` (POSIX), `grep(pattern, {cwd?, glob?, maxResults?, ignoreCase?})`, `glob(pattern, {cwd?})`, `projectRoot`, `tools`, `describeTool`, `image(handleOrPath)`; `import()` modules under projectRoot. A call that produced images returns `{text, images}`; `await image(images[0])` attaches one to your result.

description.description: Short user-facing description of what this program does.

timeout.description: Optional execution timeout in milliseconds (1000–1200000, default 120000). It includes time spent in tool calls, not time waiting for approval.

tools.description: A powerful search tool built on ripgrep. Supports full regex syntax, file filtering with glob or type, and multiple output modes. Results respect nested .gitignore files by default; pass noIgnore to include ignored files.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match. Requires output_mode: "content".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match. Requires output_mode: "content".

-C.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match. Requires output_mode: "content".

-n.description: Show line numbers in output. Defaults to true.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N entries.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where patterns can span lines. Default: false.

noIgnore.description: Search files ignored by .gitignore too. Default false.

offset.description: Skip first N entries before applying head_limit.

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines, "files_with_matches" shows file paths (default), "count" shows match counts.

path.description: File or directory to search in. Defaults to current working directory.

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

type.description: File type to search (e.g., js, py, go, rust). More efficient than glob for standard file types.

tools.description: Run one focused sub-task in an isolated sub-conversation; only its last message returns. The child cannot see this conversation, so `prompt` must be self-contained. The user can open a thread and work in it: talk to it, approve its plan or tool calls, answer its questions, carry it on after it finishes — and what it does later also reports back here. So a task the user wants to steer themselves belongs in a thread too. `resultSpec` says what the final message must contain; `goal` is only the UI label. Every result opens with the thread's session name — pass it back as `session` to continue that thread. One task per thread, never a task list, and never tell it to spawn threads of its own.

goal.description: Very short, single-line, user-facing label (for example, "Trace auth flow"). No instructions, background, or output requirements here.

prompt.description: The complete, self-contained task: every relevant fact, path, symbol, decision, and constraint. The required shape of the answer goes in `resultSpec`, not here.

resultSpec.description: Optional return contract for the child's last message: what it must contain and how to structure it (for example, "each match as `file:line — description`"). Do not repeat the task here.

session.description: Optional session name of a thread you already ran here: your prompt continues that thread, which keeps everything it has read and worked out. Omit it to start a fresh thread.

todos.description: The complete todo list — replaces the previous one in full.

tools.description:
Fetch a URL. Two modes, chosen by whether you pass `prompt`:
• RAW (omit `prompt`) — the content itself, verbatim (HTML converted to markdown; .md/.txt/JSON/source as-is). Use whenever you want to read the content.
• EXTRACT (pass `prompt`) — a sub-agent reads the page and returns ONLY a lossy answer to your prompt; the page never enters this conversation. Only for large/noisy pages where you want one specific fact.
Default to RAW. 15-minute cache.

goal.description: Very short, single-line, user-facing label for EXTRACT mode (for example, "Find release date"). Ignored in RAW mode.

prompt.description: Leave UNSET to read the content (RAW). Set ONLY to ask one question about a large, noisy page you do not want in your context — the answer is a lossy summary, so never set it for a file you mean to read, quote, or work with (.md, .txt, JSON, source).

session.description: Optional WebFetch session name returned by an earlier EXTRACT call. Set it to continue that same page-reading session; ignored in RAW mode.

url.description: The URL to fetch content from
